pos: a. and v. (drawn, as a bow made ready to shoot; used of the wicked preparing against the upright, and once, terribly, of God against Zion)
etymology: From Old English bendan, to bend a bow — the original English sense of the verb is specifically to string and draw a bow. The Hebrew is darak, to tread, since an ancient war bow was strung by setting the foot against it and treading it down.
biblical_def: The Hebrew verb behind bent is darak, to tread — a great bow was strung by putting the foot on it, which is why Scripture speaks of treading the bow. Two parties are shown with bows bent. The wicked: “The wicked have drawn out the sword, and have bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy, and to slay such as be of upright conversation” (Psalm 37:14) — the psalm answers three verses later that their bows shall be broken. And God Himself: “If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready” (Psalm 7:12). The conditional is the mercy in that verse; the whetting and the bending wait on if he turn not. Isaiah shows the Assyrian coming with “all their bows bent” (Isaiah 5:28), the instrument of the same judgment. The most painful occurrence is in Lamentations, where the bow is bent by the covenant God against His own city: “He hath bent his bow like an enemy: he stood with his right hand as an adversary, and slew all that were pleasant to the eye in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion” (Lamentations 2:4). Jeremiah does not soften it, and the book's great confession of mercies that are new every morning stands in the very next chapter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bent as incurvated, made crooked, or inclined — and notes the bow drawn and ready as the original sense.
webster_full: BENT, pp. of bend. Incurvated; made crooked; inclined; prone; having a fixed propensity; determined.
BEND, v.t. To strain, or to crook by straining; as, to bend a bow.
2. To crook; to make crooked; to curve; to inflect.
BENT, n. The state of being curving, crooked, or inclined from a straight line.
2. Declivity; as the bent of a hill. 3. Inclination; disposition; a leaning or bias of mind.
scriptures: Psalm 7:12
If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready.
Psalm 37:14
The wicked have drawn out the sword, and have bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy, and to slay such as be of upright conversation.
Isaiah 5:28
Whose arrows are sharp, and all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs shall be counted like flint, and their wheels like a whirlwind:
Lamentations 2:4

He hath bent his bow like an enemy: he stood with his right hand as an adversary, and slew all that were pleasant to the eye in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion: he poured out his fury like fire.
corruption_summary: The wrath of God is treated as an emotion unworthy of Him, so Psalm 7:12 and Lamentations 2:4 are read as ancient projection rather than revelation.
corruption_paragraphs: The standing modern objection is that a God of love could not be described bending a bow against anyone, least of all His own people, and that such texts record Israel's projection of its experience onto heaven. The doctrine of divine impassibility, rightly held, does not help that objection at all — it means God is not moved by passions as creatures are, not that He has no settled and holy opposition to sin. Scripture is unembarrassed. Lamentations 2 is an inspired poem in which the prophet says outright that the LORD stood as an adversary against Zion, and Jeremiah is not correcting a mistaken view; he is confessing a righteous judgment his people had been warned of for a century.

What must not be lost is the shape of Psalm 7:12. If he turn not — the bow is bent and the condition is stated, which is what a warning is. God announces His judgments in advance, and the announcement is itself an act of mercy; Nineveh had forty days and used them. The same book of Lamentations that says he hath bent his bow like an enemy says in the next chapter that His compassions fail not and are new every morning, and both are the voice of one man in one week. A theology that can hold only one of those sentences has not understood either.
roots_summary: Hebrew darak, to tread — and so to string a bow; Psalm 7:12, 37:14, Lamentations 2:4; qesheth, a bow; chets, an arrow — Isaiah 5:28.
roots_lines: Hebrew darak — to tread; used of stringing a bow by treading it, hence bent.
Hebrew qesheth — a bow; the weapon in every occurrence of the word.
Hebrew chets — an arrow; Isaiah 5:28, “whose arrows are sharp.”
Hebrew latash — to whet or sharpen; Psalm 7:12, of the sword.
Old English bendan — originally to string and draw a bow, not merely to curve.
usage: “He hath bent his bow, and made it ready” — and the verse begins if he turn not.
“The wicked… have bent their bow” — and the psalm answers that it shall be broken.
“He hath bent his bow like an enemy” — Lamentations, three verses from the new mercies.

pos: n. (narrowness, the pressing confinement of a siege; the covenant-curse word for a people shut up until they eat their own children)
etymology: From strait — Latin strictus, drawn tight, through Old French estreit — with -ness. Not related to straight. The Hebrew is matsoq or matsor, from tsur, to confine or besiege.
biblical_def: Straitness means narrowness — the condition of being pressed in with no room — and Scripture uses it chiefly of a besieged city. It appears in the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 with a horror the modern reader is tempted to skip: “And thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters, which the LORD thy God hath given thee, in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee” (Deuteronomy 28:53), and again in verse 55. Jeremiah announces the same thing as imminent (Jeremiah 19:9), and 2 Kings 6 records it happening in Samaria. This is not rhetoric; it is what starvation inside walls did to ancient cities, and Moses set it down eight centuries before Jerusalem experienced it. Against all that stands Elihu's picture of deliverance, which uses the word to describe what God removes: “Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness” (Job 36:16). The movement from strait to broad place is one of Scripture's standing figures for salvation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines straitness as narrowness, strictness, distress, difficulty, or want — and cites the scriptural use of a besieged people.
webster_full: STRAITNESS, n. Narrowness; as the straitness of a place.
2. Strictness; rigor; as the straitness of a man's proceedings.
3. Distress; difficulty; pressure from necessity of any kind, particularly from poverty.
STRAIT, a. Narrow; close; not broad.
Strait is the gate and narrow is the way that leadeth to life. Matt. 7.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 28:53

And thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters, which the LORD thy God hath given thee, in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee:
Deuteronomy 28:55

So that he will not give to any of them of the flesh of his children whom he shall eat: because he hath nothing left him in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee in all thy gates.
Jeremiah 19:9

And I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and they shall eat every one the flesh of his friend in the siege and straitness, wherewith their enemies, and they that seek their lives, shall straiten them.
Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness.
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 28 is dismissed as barbaric or written after the fact, which removes both the warning and the evidence of predictive prophecy.
corruption_paragraphs: Two moves are commonly made against these verses. The first is moral: a God who threatens such things is judged unworthy of worship, and the passage is set aside as belonging to a cruder stage of religion. The second is critical: the specificity of the curses is taken as proof that Deuteronomy was composed after the events it describes, during or after the exile, and dressed as prophecy. The dictionary rejects both. Mosaic authorship is the position of our Lord and the apostles, and the accuracy of the warning is exactly what a covenant document is for — the curses were published so that the people would know what they were choosing. Moses says as much in the same chapter: these things come because thou hearkenedst not unto the voice of the LORD thy God.

The moral objection deserves a plainer answer than it usually gets. Deuteronomy 28 does not describe God feeding children to their parents; it describes what happens to a walled city under siege when the covenant protection is withdrawn, and the withdrawal is announced centuries in advance with the express purpose of preventing it. The whole apparatus of prophetic warning — the repeated sendings, the rising early and sending, the long delay of judgment — is mercy operating in the open. Job 36:16 shows the direction God prefers: out of the strait into a broad place, with a table full of fatness.
roots_summary: Hebrew matsoq, straitness or distress — Deuteronomy 28:53; matsor, a siege — the companion word; tsur, to bind or besiege; merchab, a broad place — Job 36:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew matsoq — straitness, anguish, the pressure of confinement; Deuteronomy 28:53 and 55.
Hebrew matsor — a siege, an entrenchment; joined to matsoq in the curse formula.
Hebrew tsur — to confine, to besiege; the root of both nouns.
Hebrew merchab — a broad place; Job 36:16 and Psalm 18:19, the opposite of straitness.
Latin strictus, drawn tight — the root of English strait, unrelated to straight.
usage: “In the siege, and in the straitness” — the covenant curse stated plainly, centuries early.
“Out of the strait into a broad place” — the standing figure for deliverance.
“Strait is the gate” — the same root, of the narrow way to life.

pos: adv. (with weight, sorrowfully, with difficulty; of David mourning for enemies, and of Babylon's yoke laid on the aged)
etymology: From heavy — Old English hefig, weighty — with -ly. The Hebrew at Psalm 35:14 is qadar, to be dark or to mourn in black; at Isaiah 47:6 the verb is kabad, to be heavy, the same root as kabod, glory.
biblical_def: David describes his conduct toward men who later repaid him with slander: “I behaved myself as though he had been my friend or brother: I bowed down heavily, as one that mourneth for his mother” (Psalm 35:14). The Hebrew qadar means to be dark, and it is the word for the mourner's blackened garments and unwashed face. David says he grieved for the sickness of men who, in his own calamity, gathered themselves against him and rejoiced. This is the psalm our Lord quotes concerning those who hated Him without a cause, and the conduct David describes is precisely what the Sermon on the Mount later commands. The other occurrence is a rebuke of an instrument that exceeded its commission: “I was wroth with my people, I have polluted mine inheritance, and given them into thine hand: thou didst shew them no mercy; upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke” (Isaiah 47:6). Babylon was God's appointed rod, and Babylon is judged for the manner of her striking — for showing no mercy and for laying a heavy yoke on old men. That God uses a wicked nation does not excuse the nation, and Isaiah 47 is the proof.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heavily as with great weight, with grief or sorrow, and as with difficulty or slowly.
webster_full: HEAVILY, adv. With great weight; as, to bear heavily on a thing.
2. Grievously; oppressively.
The hand of God pressed heavily upon them.
3. Sorrowfully; with grief.
4. With an air of dejection; as, to look heavily. 5. Slowly and laboriously; with difficulty.
scriptures: Psalm 35:14
I behaved myself as though he had been my friend or brother: I bowed down heavily, as one that mourneth for his mother.
Isaiah 47:6
I was wroth with my people, I have polluted mine inheritance, and given them into thine hand: thou didst shew them no mercy; upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke.
Psalm 38:6
I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long.
Psalm 35:13
But as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth: I humbled my soul with fasting; and my prayer returned into mine own bosom.
corruption_summary: Grief has been given a schedule and a set of stages, and the biblical practice of open, bodily, public mourning is treated as unhealthy excess.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern grief is expected to be private, brief, and progressive — passing through stages toward a resolution, with prolonged sorrow classed as a disorder. Scripture's mourners are none of those things. David wears sackcloth, fasts, blackens himself, and bows down heavily, and he does it publicly for men who hated him. Job's friends sat with him seven days and said nothing. Jesus wept at a grave He was about to open. There is nothing in the Bible corresponding to the expectation that a sorrow should be finished by a certain date, and much that assumes the opposite — the Psalms of lament are the largest single category in the psalter and several of them do not resolve. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic frame in order to rebut it

Isaiah 47:6 addresses a different and harder question: what to make of the human agent of a divinely-appointed affliction. Babylon was raised up to chastise Judah, and Babylon is judged — for cruelty beyond her commission, for showing no mercy, for a yoke laid heavily on the ancient. The Reformed doctrine of concurrence is exactly here: God ordains the end and the means, and the wicked means remains fully culpable for the wickedness it freely chose. Joseph's brothers meant it for evil; God meant it unto good; both clauses are true, and neither cancels the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew qadar, to be dark, to mourn — Psalm 35:14; kabad, to be heavy — Isaiah 47:6; shachach, to bow down — Psalm 35:14, 38:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew qadar — to be dark, to go about blackened in mourning; Psalm 35:14.
Hebrew kabad — to be heavy or weighty; Isaiah 47:6, and the root of kabod, glory.
Hebrew shachach — to bow down, be brought low; Psalm 35:14 and 38:6.
Hebrew ol — a yoke; Isaiah 47:6, laid heavily upon the ancient.
Old English hefig — weighty; the root of the English adjective.
usage: “I bowed down heavily, as one that mourneth for his mother” — and they gathered against him.
“Upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke” — the rod judged for its manner.
“My clothing was sackcloth” — the same psalm, of grief for enemies.

pos: v. (stripped of something possessed; of Rebekah fearing the loss of both sons, of Hezekiah counting his years cut off, and of the ostrich denied wisdom by God)
etymology: From Latin deprivare, to take away from, from de- and privare, to bereave. The Hebrew at Genesis 27:45 is shakal, to be bereaved of children; at Isaiah 38:10 the verb is paqad in a passive sense, to be visited or numbered off.
biblical_def: Three very different deprivations use this word. Rebekah, having engineered the deception of Isaac, foresees its cost: “why should I be deprived also of you both in one day?” (Genesis 27:45). She expects to lose Jacob to flight and Esau to the blood-avenger, and the sentence is a mother's arithmetic on the outcome of her own scheming; the narrative never records that she saw Jacob again. Hezekiah, told to set his house in order, reckons the same way about time: “I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of the grave: I am deprived of the residue of my years” (Isaiah 38:10). His years were restored, fifteen of them, and the chapter that follows shows him receiving Babylonian envoys and showing them everything — a granted request that did his house no good. The third is the strangest and is spoken by God about a bird: “Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding” (Job 39:17), of the ostrich who leaves her eggs in the dust. It appears in the great speech from the whirlwind, and its point is that God distributes His gifts as He pleases and is answerable to no creature for the distribution.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deprive as to take from, to bereave of something possessed, and also to hinder from possessing or enjoying.
webster_full: DEPRIVED, pp. Bereft; divested; hindered; stripped of possession.
DEPRIVE, v.t. To take from; to bereave of something possessed or enjoyed; followed by of.
God hath deprived her of wisdom. Job 39.
2. To hinder from possessing or enjoying; to debar.
3. To free or release from.
scriptures: Genesis 27:45
Until thy brother's anger turn away from thee, and he forget that which thou hast done to him: then I will send, and fetch thee from thence: why should I be deprived also of you both in one day?
Isaiah 38:10
I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of the grave: I am deprived of the residue of my years.
Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding.
Isaiah 38:11
I said, I shall not see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living: I shall behold man no more with the inhabitants of the world.
corruption_summary: Deprivation is treated as an injustice by definition, so that Job 39:17 — God withholding a gift — becomes unthinkable.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary moral vocabulary treats any inequality of gift as a wrong requiring redress; to be deprived is by definition to have been treated unjustly. Job 39:17 refuses the premise in the plainest possible terms: God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding. The subject is a bird, deliberately, because the point is easier to see there before it is applied to men. God gives the horse strength and the hawk flight and the ostrich neither sense nor care for her young, and the speech from the whirlwind offers no defence of the arrangement whatever. Paul makes the same argument about men in Romans 9, and the objection he anticipates is exactly the modern one.

The doctrine is not fatalism and it is not indifference. Rebekah's loss in Genesis 27 came through her own contrivance, and Scripture lets the reader see the connection without comment. Hezekiah's deprivation was reversed in answer to prayer, and the fifteen added years produced the display to Babylon that sealed his sons' captivity — a sobering note on granted requests. What holds all three together is that God is the one who gives and withholds, and that a creature's standing to complain is the very thing Job discovered he did not have. His answer, at the end of the whirlwind, was to lay his hand on his mouth.
roots_summary: Hebrew shakal, to be bereaved of children — Genesis 27:45; paqad, to visit, number, or miss — Isaiah 38:10; nashah, to make forget — Job 39:17; Latin deprivare, to take from.
roots_lines: Hebrew shakal — to be bereaved, especially of children; Genesis 27:45.
Hebrew paqad — to visit, number, appoint or miss; Isaiah 38:10 of years cut off.
Hebrew nashah — to cause to forget, to withhold; Job 39:17 of the ostrich.
Hebrew chalaq — to apportion; the doctrine of God distributing gifts as He wills.
Latin deprivare, from privare, to bereave — the source of the English word.
usage: “Why should I be deprived also of you both in one day?” — a mother reckoning the cost of her own scheme.
“I am deprived of the residue of my years” — and fifteen were given back.
“God hath deprived her of wisdom” — stated of a bird, and offered without defence.

pos: v. and n. (driven out from a country or a presence; in 2 Samuel 14, the word on which the wise woman of Tekoah builds her plea, and on which she states a great gospel principle)
etymology: From Old French banir, to proclaim an outlaw, from a Frankish root meaning a public proclamation — the same root as ban. The Hebrew at 2 Samuel 14:13 is nadach, to be driven away or thrust out.
biblical_def: Both occurrences of the word stand in one speech, and it is one of the most theologically remarkable speeches in the Old Testament. The wise woman of Tekoah, sent by Joab, brings David a fictitious case and then turns it on him: “for the king doth speak this thing as one which is faulty, in that the king doth not fetch home again his banished” (2 Samuel 14:13). Absalom is the banished man in view. Then she says something larger than her errand: “For we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither doth God respect any person: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him” (2 Samuel 14:14). Three claims in one verse. Death is irreversible by any human power — water spilt cannot be gathered. God is no respecter of persons, so there is no favour to be traded on. And yet He devises means that His banished be not expelled from Him. The Hebrew is deliberate and the church has always read it as more than the woman knew: God contrives a way, consistent with His own justice, to bring back those driven out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines banish as to condemn to leave one's country, to drive away or compel to depart, and figuratively to expel from the mind.
webster_full: BANISHED, pp. Compelled to leave one's country; driven from a place; expelled.
BANISH, v.t. To condemn to exile, or compel to leave one's country, by authority of the prince or government, either for life or for a limited time.
2. To drive away; to compel to depart; to dispel; as, to banish sorrow.
3. To quit one's country voluntarily, and with a view to reside elsewhere.
BANISHMENT, n. The act of a prince or government, compelling a citizen to leave his country.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 14:13

And the woman said, Wherefore then hast thou thought such a thing against the people of God? for the king doth speak this thing as one which is faulty, in that the king doth not fetch home again his banished.
2 Samuel 14:14

For we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither doth God respect any person: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him.
Genesis 3:24
So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.
Ephesians 2:13
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
corruption_summary: 2 Samuel 14:14 is used to argue that God will find some way to save everyone, which reverses the verse's own careful reasoning.
corruption_paragraphs: This verse is a favourite proof text for universalism: God devises means that His banished be not expelled from Him, and the conclusion drawn is that no one is finally lost. The reading ignores what the same sentence says about God's justice — neither doth God respect any person — which is precisely the difficulty that devising means exists to answer. If God simply overlooked the offence He would be respecting persons, and the woman knows it. The whole force of the sentence is that a way had to be devised, and the New Testament names what it cost: God set forth His Son to be a propitiation, that He might be just and the justifier of him which believeth.

The narrative context is a further caution. David did fetch Absalom home, and did it badly — two years in Jerusalem without seeing the king's face, a reconciliation without repentance on one side or dealing with the offence on the other. It ended in rebellion, civil war, and the death of the son. Scripture places its greatest statement about God devising means immediately beside a human attempt at restoration that failed for want of any means at all. The first banishment is in Genesis 3, where God drove out the man and set cherubim with a flaming sword; the means devised is the blood by which those who were far off are made nigh.
roots_summary: Hebrew nadach, to be driven out, thrust away — 2 Samuel 14:13-14; chashab, to devise or reckon — the verb of God's devising; garash, to drive out — Genesis 3:24.
roots_lines: Hebrew nadach — to be driven away, banished, an outcast; 2 Samuel 14:13 and 14:14.
Hebrew chashab — to think, reckon, devise a plan; the verb behind “he devise means.”
Hebrew garash — to drive out; Genesis 3:24, the first banishment.
Hebrew nasa panim — to lift the face, to respect persons; denied of God in 14:14.
Old French banir, to proclaim an outlaw — the source of English banish and ban.
usage: “The king doth not fetch home again his banished” — the woman of Tekoah's charge.
“As water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again” — death beyond human remedy.
“Yet doth he devise means” — a way contrived that does not set aside His justice.

pos: v. (driven out by force; of the Canaanites Israel did not expel, of Anak's sons Caleb did, and of the apostles driven from Antioch's coasts)
etymology: From Latin expellere, to drive out, from ex and pellere, to drive. The Hebrew at Joshua 13:13 is yarash, to dispossess or take possession by driving out; the Greek at Acts 13:50 is ekballo, to cast out.
biblical_def: The word runs along the fault line of the conquest narratives. On the failure side: “Nevertheless the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day” (Joshua 13:13). The book of Judges opens with a whole catalogue of such failures, and the consequences run through the rest of the Old Testament — the nations left in the land became the snare God said they would be. On the obedience side stands one old man: “And they gave Hebron unto Caleb, as Moses said: and he expelled thence the three sons of Anak” (Judges 1:20). Caleb was eighty-five and asked for the hill country with the giants on it, because the LORD had promised it forty-five years earlier and he had not stopped believing it. In the New Testament the direction reverses and the church is on the receiving end: “the Jews stirred up the devout and honourable women, and the chief men of the city, and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts” (Acts 13:50). Luke adds immediately that the disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines expel as to drive or force out, to eject, and also to banish or exclude from a society.
webster_full: EXPELLED, pp. Driven out or away; forced to leave; banished; exiled; ejected.
EXPEL, v.t. To drive or force out from any inclosed place; as, to expel wind from the stomach.
2. To drive out; to force to leave; to eject; as, to expel an enemy from a country.
3. To banish; to exile; to force to quit a country.
4. To exclude; to keep out or off; as, to expel a member of a society.
scriptures: Joshua 13:13
Nevertheless the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day.
Judges 1:20
And they gave Hebron unto Caleb, as Moses said: and he expelled thence the three sons of Anak.
Acts 13:50
But the Jews stirred up the devout and honourable women, and the chief men of the city, and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts.
Acts 13:52
And the disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: The conquest is judged by modern political categories, and the far more relevant lesson — what Israel's incomplete obedience cost — is left unpreached.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary discussion of Joshua fixes almost entirely on the morality of the conquest, and the church has often been more anxious about that question than the text is. Scripture's own framing is judicial: the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full in Abraham's day and was full four hundred years later; the land is said to spew out its inhabitants for their abominations, and Israel is warned in the same breath that it will spew her out too if she does the same. The conquest is presented as an act of divine judgment executed by a commissioned instrument, not as a national land grab with a religious excuse, and the identical judgment fell on Israel when she earned it.

The lesson the church most needs from these texts is the one about incompleteness. They expelled not — and the peoples left in the land became exactly the snare the LORD had said they would be, drawing Israel into the idolatry that ended in exile. Every generation of believers has its Geshurites: sins not driven out but tolerated at the border, on the reasoning that they are small, or useful, or too costly to remove. Caleb is the counter-example and he is instructive precisely because his portion was the hardest — the hill country, with the giants — and he took it at eighty-five on the strength of a promise made when he was forty.
roots_summary: Hebrew yarash, to dispossess — Joshua 13:13; garash, to drive out — Judges 1:20; Greek ekballo, to cast out — Acts 13:50; Latin expellere, to drive out.
roots_lines: Hebrew yarash — to take possession by dispossessing; Joshua 13:13, the word of the conquest.
Hebrew garash — to drive out, expel; Judges 1:20 of Caleb and the sons of Anak.
Hebrew Anaqim — the Anakim, the giants whose report frightened ten of the twelve spies.
Greek ekballo — to cast out; Acts 13:50, of Paul and Barnabas driven from the coasts.
Latin expellere, from pellere, to drive — the source of the English word.
usage: “The children of Israel expelled not” — and the nations left became the snare foretold.
“He expelled thence the three sons of Anak” — Caleb at eighty-five, on a promise forty-five years old.
“Expelled them out of their coasts” — and the disciples were filled with joy.

pos: v. (entered a territory in force; of the Philistines and Amalekites upon Israel, and of the Moabite bands that came in at the year's turn)
etymology: From Latin invadere, to go into, from in and vadere, to go. The Hebrew at 1 Samuel 30:1 is pashat, to strip or spread out — the raiding party spreading over the country; the Authorized Version's margin at 1 Samuel 23:27 renders it “spread themselves upon.”
biblical_def: The Hebrew verb pictures a raiding force spreading over open country like a stain, and the Authorized Version uses it of the recurring plague of Israel's history. The most important occurrence is the sacking of Ziklag: “when David and his men were come to Ziklag on the third day, that the Amalekites had invaded the south, and Ziklag, and smitten Ziklag, and burned it with fire” (1 Samuel 30:1). What follows is one of the great hinges of David's life. Everything he had was gone, the wives and children of his men were taken, and “David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him… but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God” (1 Samuel 30:6). That last clause is one of the plainest statements in Scripture of what a believer does when there is no comfort available from any other quarter. Elsewhere the word marks the ordinary insecurity of a small nation: “the bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year” (2 Kings 13:20), raiding being seasonal; and Ahaz's reign is measured by it, with the Philistines taking city after city of the low country (2 Chronicles 28:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines invade as to enter a country as an enemy with a view to conquest or plunder, and figuratively to attack or infringe.
webster_full: INVADED, pp. Entered by an enemy; attacked; encroached on.
INVADE, v.t. To enter a country, as an army with hostile intentions; to enter as an enemy, with a view to conquest or plunder.
2. To attack; to assail; to assault.
3. To attack; to infringe; to encroach on; to violate; as, the king invaded the rights of the people.
INVASION, n. A hostile entrance into the possessions of another.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 30:1
And it came to pass, when David and his men were come to Ziklag on the third day, that the Amalekites had invaded the south, and Ziklag, and smitten Ziklag, and burned it with fire;
1 Samuel 30:6

And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God.
2 Kings 13:20
And Elisha died, and they buried him. And the bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year.
2 Chronicles 28:18

The Philistines also had invaded the cities of the low country, and of the south of Judah, and had taken Bethshemesh, and Ajalon, and Gederoth, and Shocho with the villages thereof, and Timnah with the villages thereof, Gimzo also and the villages thereof: and they dwelt there.
corruption_summary: 1 Samuel 30:6 is quoted as a slogan for self-motivation, when the verse says David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.
corruption_paragraphs: David encouraged himself in the LORD his God is regularly cited as an early instance of positive self-talk — a man rallying his own spirits. The preposition is the whole verse. He did not encourage himself with a recollection of past successes or with confidence in his own resources; he strengthened himself in the LORD, and the next verse shows what that meant practically: he called for Abiathar the priest and the ephod and enquired of the LORD whether to pursue. The strengthening produced immediate submission of the decision to God, not a resolve to act on his own judgment. That is the difference between biblical encouragement and morale.

The circumstances are worth stating plainly, because they are extreme. David's city was burnt, his two wives taken, his six hundred men bereaved of their families, and those same men, his only remaining asset, were discussing stoning him. He had also brought the situation partly on himself by his long sojourn among the Philistines. There is no comfort available anywhere in that scene except in God, which is why the verse has served believers for three thousand years. The chapter ends with everything recovered, nothing lacking, small or great, and David establishing a statute for the division of spoil between those who fought and those who stayed with the stuff.
roots_summary: Hebrew pashat, to strip, spread out, make a raid — 1 Samuel 30:1, 2 Kings 13:20; gedud, a raiding band — 2 Kings 13:20; chazaq, to strengthen — 1 Samuel 30:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew pashat — to strip off, to spread out in a raid; the verb rendered invaded.
Hebrew gedud — a troop or raiding band; 2 Kings 13:20, of the Moabites.
Hebrew chazaq — to be strong, to strengthen oneself; 1 Samuel 30:6.
Hebrew Amaleq — Amalek, the hereditary enemy from Exodus 17 onward.
Latin invadere, to go in — the source of the English word.
usage: “The Amalekites had invaded the south” — and Ziklag was burnt with fire.
“David encouraged himself in the LORD his God” — the preposition carries the verse.
“At the coming in of the year” — raiding was seasonal, and expected.

pos: v. (to lessen or take from; the standing prohibition against subtracting from God's word, and the law protecting a wife's maintenance)
etymology: From Latin diminuere, to lessen, from de- and minuere, to make small. The Hebrew at Deuteronomy 4:2 is gara, to shave off, withdraw, or restrain — the same verb used of trimming a beard.
biblical_def: The most consequential use is the double command that frames the giving of the law. “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you” (Deuteronomy 4:2), repeated at the close of the same discourse: “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32). Jeremiah receives the same charge for his own preaching: “speak unto them all the words that I command thee to speak unto them; diminish not a word” (Jeremiah 26:2) — and the words in question were the ones that nearly got him killed that same day. The Revelation closes the canon with the identical formula. The word also protects the weak in a law of great practical mercy: if a man takes a second wife, “her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish” (Exodus 21:10). The Mosaic legislation regulates polygamy without commending it, and this statute exists to prevent a first wife being quietly starved out of a household — the maintenance is not reducible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines diminish as to lessen, to make less or smaller by any means, and notes it is opposed to increase and augment.
webster_full: DIMINISH, v.t. To lessen; to make less or smaller, by any means; opposed to increase and augment; as, to diminish the size of a thing.
2. To lessen; to impair; to degrade.
Neither shall ye diminish ought from it. Deut. 4.
3. To take away or subtract.
DIMINUTION, n. The act of lessening; a making smaller; opposed to increase or augmentation.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
Deuteronomy 12:32
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Jeremiah 26:2

Thus saith the LORD; Stand in the court of the LORD'S house, and speak unto all the cities of Judah, which come to worship in the LORD'S house, all the words that I command thee to speak unto them; diminish not a word:
Exodus 21:10
If he take him another wife; her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish.
corruption_summary: Diminishing is now done by omission rather than excision — the hard texts kept in the Bible and dropped from the pulpit.
corruption_paragraphs: No conservative church cuts verses out of Scripture, and the prohibition of Deuteronomy 4:2 is therefore assumed to be satisfied. It is not. A word may be diminished as effectively by never preaching it as by deleting it, and every generation has its unpreached portions — the imprecatory psalms, the judgment texts, the passages on church discipline, the hard sayings about money, the whole of the creation and conquest narratives, the doctrine of hell. Jeremiah 26:2 is the exact case, since the words God told him not to diminish were the ones the congregation would least tolerate, and the priests and prophets laid hold on him that same hour saying Thou shalt surely die. The charge diminish not a word was given precisely because he would be tempted to.

The other half of the command deserves equal attention. Adding to the word is Rome's historic error — tradition raised to equal authority, doctrines defined without scriptural warrant, ordinances multiplied — and it is also the error of every modern movement that supplements the canon with fresh revelation. The two halves together are the substance of sola Scriptura: nothing may be added and nothing subtracted, because the sufficiency of Scripture is a claim about a fixed text. Exodus 21:10 shows the same principle applied to a household; what is owed to the weak may not be quietly reduced.
roots_summary: Hebrew gara, to shave off, withdraw, diminish — Deuteronomy 4:2, 12:32, Exodus 21:10; yasaph, to add — the paired verb; Latin diminuere, to lessen.
roots_lines: Hebrew gara — to shave off, take away, restrain; the verb of Deuteronomy 4:2 and Exodus 21:10.
Hebrew yasaph — to add, increase; the paired prohibition in the same verses.
Hebrew onah — the duty of marriage; the third item a husband may not diminish.
Greek aphaireo — to take away; Revelation 22:19, closing the canon with the same formula.
Latin diminuere, from minuere, to make small — the source of the English word.
usage: “Ye shall not add… neither shall ye diminish” — the two halves of sola Scriptura.
“Diminish not a word” — said of the sermon that nearly cost Jeremiah his life.
“Shall he not diminish” — a wife's maintenance made non-reducible by statute.

pos: n. (darkness and heaviness together; twice, and only in the fixed prophetic formula for the day of the LORD)
etymology: From gloom — Middle English gloumen, to look sullen — with -ness. The Hebrew is aphelah, thick darkness, from a root meaning to be dusky; the formula pairs it with choshek, darkness, and araphel, thick cloud.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice, and both times inside the same four-fold prophetic formula for the day of the LORD. Joel: “A day of darkness and of gloominess, a day of clouds and of thick darkness, as the morning spread upon the mountains: a great people and a strong; there hath not been ever the like” (Joel 2:2). Zephaniah, independently: “That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness and desolation, a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness” (Zephaniah 1:15). Two prophets, separated in time, reach for an identical stack of terms, which suggests a fixed liturgical or prophetic form. The imagery is deliberately the reverse of creation and of Sinai: where God came down in cloud and darkness to give a covenant, He comes in the same cloud and darkness to prosecute it. Amos had already destroyed the popular assumption that the day would be Israel's vindication: “Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD! to what end is it for you? the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light” (Amos 5:18). Zephaniah adds that it is near and hasteth greatly (Zephaniah 1:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gloominess as want of light, obscurity, and also darkness of prospect or aspect, want of cheerfulness.
webster_full: GLOOMINESS, n. Want of light; obscurity; darkness; dismalness.
2. Want of cheerfulness; cloudiness of look; heaviness of mind; melancholy.
A gloominess of temper.
GLOOM, n. Obscurity; partial or total darkness; thick shade.
2. Cloudiness or heaviness of mind; melancholy; aspect of sorrow.
scriptures: Joel 2:2

A day of darkness and of gloominess, a day of clouds and of thick darkness, as the morning spread upon the mountains: a great people and a strong; there hath not been ever the like, neither shall be any more after it, even to the years of many generations.
Zephaniah 1:15
That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness and desolation, a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness,
Amos 5:18
Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD! to what end is it for you? the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light.
Zephaniah 1:14
The great day of the LORD is near, it is near, and hasteth greatly, even the voice of the day of the LORD: the mighty man shall cry there bitterly.
corruption_summary: The day of the LORD is assumed to be good news for everyone who is religious, which is precisely the assumption Amos was sent to destroy.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel in Amos's day looked forward to the day of the LORD as a national vindication — the moment their God would settle accounts with the nations in their favour. Amos told them it would be darkness and not light, and that for them it would be as if a man fled from a lion and a bear met him. The assumption he was attacking is alive in every generation of religious people: that being on the right side of the institutional line guarantees a favourable verdict. Zephaniah and Joel both put gloominess in the formula for the same reason, and Joel adds the only appropriate response — turn ye even to me with all your heart, and rend your heart, and not your garments.

The opposite corruption is to make the day of the LORD entirely a matter of dates and identifications. The prophetic texts describe a day characterised by wrath, trouble, distress, wasteness, desolation, darkness, gloominess, cloud, and thick darkness, and none of those words is a chronological marker. Joel's locusts were a present judgment and a figure of a greater one; Peter at Pentecost quotes Joel of his own day; the New Testament sets the final day at Christ's appearing. The pastoral use of the doctrine is not calculation but preparation, and Joel supplies the promise that makes preparation reasonable: He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.
roots_summary: Hebrew aphelah, thick darkness — Joel 2:2, Zephaniah 1:15; choshek, darkness; araphel, thick cloud; anan, cloud — the four terms of the formula.
roots_lines: Hebrew aphelah — thick or gloomy darkness; the word rendered gloominess in both prophets.
Hebrew choshek — darkness; the first term of the fourfold formula.
Hebrew araphel — heavy cloud, thick darkness; also of Sinai in Exodus 20:21.
Hebrew anan — a cloud; the same word as the cloudy pillar of the exodus.
Hebrew yom YHWH — the day of the LORD; the subject of the whole formula.
usage: “A day of darkness and of gloominess” — Joel and Zephaniah use the identical stack of terms.
“The day of the LORD is darkness, and not light” — Amos against the popular expectation.
“It is near, and hasteth greatly” — the note of urgency in the formula.

pos: n. (hurt, loss, injury sustained; of a king's revenue, of Paul's foreseen shipwreck, and of a rebuke that cost the Corinthians nothing)
etymology: From Latin damnum, loss or penalty, through Old French damage — the same root as damn and condemn, all of which begin in the idea of loss imposed. The Greek at 2 Corinthians 7:9 is zemioo, to suffer loss.
biblical_def: Three uses, and the last is the doctrinally weighty one. The Persian court weighs it commercially: “Take heed now that ye fail not to do this: why should damage grow to the hurt of the kings?” (Ezra 4:22) — the argument that persuaded Artaxerxes to stop the building of Jerusalem was a projected loss of revenue. Paul uses it of a voyage he had judged rightly and been overruled on: “Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage, not only of the lading and ship, but also of our lives” (Acts 27:10). The centurion believed the master and owner rather than Paul, and the ship was lost as Paul said, though every life was spared. The great use is pastoral: “Now I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner, that ye might receive damage by us in nothing” (2 Corinthians 7:9). Paul had written a severe letter, it had grieved them, and he is stating the aim of severity in the ministry: that the sorrow should be godly, produce repentance, and leave the church without loss. He explains the distinction in the next verse — godly sorrow works repentance unto salvation, the sorrow of the world works death.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines damage as any hurt, injury, or harm to person, character, or estate — and in law the value in money of a loss sustained.
webster_full: DAMAGE, n. Any hurt, injury or harm to one's person or estate.
2. The value in money of what is lost; equivalent for injury sustained.
3. In law, the estimated reparation in money for detriment or injury sustained.
DAMAGE, v.t. To hurt or harm; to injure; to impair; to lessen the soundness, goodness or value of.
DAMAGEABLE, a. That may be injured or impaired; susceptible of damage.
scriptures: Ezra 4:22
Take heed now that ye fail not to do this: why should damage grow to the hurt of the kings?
Acts 27:10
And said unto them, Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage, not only of the lading and ship, but also of our lives.
2 Corinthians 7:9
Now I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner, that ye might receive damage by us in nothing.
2 Corinthians 7:10
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
corruption_summary: Any sorrow caused by correction is now counted as damage done, which makes the godly sorrow of 2 Corinthians 7 impossible to administer.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning assumption is that if a word causes pain it has caused harm, and that the measure of the harm is the pain reported. Paul's language cuts directly across it. He made them sorry, he says so plainly, and he adds that he does not repent of it — and the whole point of the passage is that they received damage in nothing. Sorrow and damage are distinguished, and the distinguishing mark is what the sorrow produces. Godly sorrow works repentance unto salvation; worldly sorrow works death. A ministry that will never grieve anyone has disarmed itself of the only instrument by which Paul recovered the Corinthian church. # voice-lock-ok: harmful: names the harm-only standard in order to rebut it

Two guards belong on this doctrine. First, Paul's severity was exercised with visible reluctance — out of much affliction and anguish of heart, with many tears, and not to grieve them but that they might know his love. Severity administered without that cost to the one administering it is not the apostolic pattern. Second, the aim is stated and is measurable: repentance, carefulness, clearing of themselves, indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, revenge. Paul checks the fruit. A rebuke that produces only compliance, resentment, or a sullen silence has not achieved what he means, and the man who gave it should not comfort himself that the pain proves the point.
roots_summary: Aramaic nezaq, damage or loss — Ezra 4:22; Greek zemia, loss — Acts 27:10; zemioo, to suffer loss — 2 Corinthians 7:9; Latin damnum, loss.
roots_lines: Aramaic nezaq — damage, injury, loss of revenue; Ezra 4:22.
Greek zemia — loss, damage; Acts 27:10, and Philippians 3:7, where Paul counts his gains loss.
Greek zemioo — to suffer loss; 2 Corinthians 7:9, and Mark 8:36 of losing one's own soul.
Greek lupe — sorrow, grief; the word Paul distinguishes into godly and worldly.
Latin damnum, loss or penalty — the root of damage, damn, and condemn.
usage: “Why should damage grow to the hurt of the kings?” — revenue, and the work stopped.
“This voyage will be with hurt and much damage” — Paul overruled, and right.
“That ye might receive damage by us in nothing” — sorrow caused, damage avoided.
